title: Arrays, std::string and std::string_view
objectives: Declare, index and iterate C-style arrays, and explain array-to-pointer decay
Manipulate std::string: construction, concatenation, size and element access
Use std::string_view for non-owning read-only text and avoid dangling views
Choose between array, std::string and std::string_view for a given job
motivation: Market data arrives as text - 'AAPL', 'BUY', 'MSFT-0621-C190' - and positions live in fixed-size buffers inside hot loops. Choosing the wrong tool here costs nanoseconds per tick or crashes via out-of-bounds indexing. This lesson covers the raw array C++ inherits from C, the owning std::string, and C++17's zero-copy std::string_view.

blocks.md: A C-style array declares N elements of one type in **contiguous** memory: `double fills[4];`. Elements are indexed from 0 to N-1; there is **no bounds check**, and an out-of-bounds index is undefined behaviour, not an exception. In the scope where the array is declared you can recover its element count with the sizeof ratio `sizeof(fills) / sizeof(fills[0])` - but pass the array to a function and it **decays** to a pointer to its first element, forgetting its length entirely. That is why C-style APIs always carry a separate count parameter (you saw `const int* values, int count` in a previous exercise). Iteration is either a classic index loop or a range-for over the elements.

blocks.caption: The sizeof ratio works here because fills' true array type is known in this scope. Output: 30 then 5
int fills[5] is 20 contiguous bytes, four per int - contiguity is what makes element i addressable as base + i * sizeof(int).

blocks.md: **std::string** owns a resizable character buffer: it manages its own memory, knows its length via `size()`, concatenates with `+` and `+=`, compares with `==` and `<`, and indexes like an array (`s[0]` is the first character). It copies when passed by value and allocates as it grows - the price you pay for safety and convenience. A literal such as "FILL" in your source is really a C-style `const char[5]` array; assigning it to a std::string copies those bytes into the string's own buffer. Note that `==` on two std::strings compares *contents*, whereas `==` on two C-style arrays would compare addresses - a subtle but critical difference.

blocks.caption: std::string grows its own buffer; size() counts characters. Output: filled 6

blocks.md: **std::string_view** is a pointer plus a length: a read-only window over text it does **not** own. Passing a string_view costs no allocation and no copy regardless of the text's length, and it accepts std::string, string literals or slices taken with `substr` - which is why it has become the default parameter type for read-only text in C++17 codebases. The trade-off is lifetime: the view is valid only as long as the underlying buffer exists. Slicing with `substr` produces a view *into the original buffer*, not a new copy, and `find` returns the special value `npos` when nothing matches - so `substr(0, s.find('-'))` means 'everything before the first dash, or the whole text if there is no dash'.

blocks.caption: Zero-copy slicing: the view points into the caller's buffer. Output: MSFT then SPY

blocks.title: The dangling view
blocks.md: `std::string_view bad() { std::string local = "AAPL"; return local; }` returns a window over a buffer destroyed when the function exits; every later use is undefined behaviour. Views **borrow** - they never extend a lifetime. The same rule you learned for references applies: an alias may never outlive its object.

guidedExercise.prompt: Write a function `double meanFills(const double* values, std::size_t n)` and call it on `double fills[4] = {101.5, 102.25, 99.75, 103.0};`. What does the program print, and why does the function need `n` as a separate parameter?
hints: Inside the function, `values` is just a pointer - the array's length did not travel with it (decay!).

independentExercise.prompt:
Build a small symbol utility with std::string_view:

- `std::size_t dashCount(std::string_view s)` returns the number of '-' characters.
- `std::string_view optionRoot(std::string_view s)` returns the text before the first '-' (or the whole view if there is none).

Run both functions on "MSFT-0621-C190" and "SPY" and give all four results, plus the full compilable program.
hints: Loop i from 0 to s.size() and inspect s[i] == '-'.
string_view::find returns npos when nothing matches; substr(0, npos) means 'to the end'.

commonMistakes: Indexing past the end of a raw array - there is no bounds check and out-of-bounds access is undefined behaviour.
Using sizeof(fills)/sizeof(fills[0]) inside a function that received the array - it decayed to a pointer, so the ratio is meaningless.
Returning a std::string_view of a local std::string - the view dangles the moment the string dies.
Comparing C-style char arrays with == and comparing addresses instead of contents; == compares text only for std::string and string_view.
Passing std::string by value in a hot loop when a const std::string& or std::string_view would not copy at all.
realWorldApplication: Protocol parsers and log scanners take string_view parameters to slice messages without a single allocation; owning std::strings appear only where text must be stored beyond the call.
quantFinanceApplication: A market-data handler decoding 'MSFT-0621-C190' into root, expiry and strike uses string_view slices over the incoming buffer - zero copies in the hottest path of the feed.
summary: C arrays are fixed-size, contiguous and unchecked; they decay to pointers at function boundaries, losing their length.
std::string owns a resizable buffer with size(), += concatenation and value-semantic (content) comparisons.
std::string_view (C++17) is a non-owning pointer+length read-only window: cheap to pass, fatal to outlive its buffer.
The sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) element-count trick works only where the array's true type is still known.
Default to string_view for read-only parameters, std::string for owned text, raw arrays for fixed-size hot data.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++17 program print?
quiz.explanation: The loop sums 2+4+6+8+10 = 30. sizeof(a) is 20 bytes and sizeof(a[0]) is 4, so the ratio is 5 - valid because a's true array type is known in this scope.

quiz.prompt: You pass `fills` (declared as int[5]) to a function taking `int* arr`. Inside the function, what does sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) evaluate to?
options: 2 on a 64-bit machine - the array length was lost in decay
quiz.explanation: The array decayed to a pointer, so sizeof(arr) is the pointer size (8 bytes) and the ratio is 8/4 = 2 - not the element count. The length must travel as a separate parameter.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++17 program print?
quiz.explanation: += appends "ed" to "fill" producing "filled", whose size() is 6 characters.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about std::string_view is TRUE?
options: It copies the text it views
It owns the buffer it points at
It is a read-only pointer+length pair that never allocates
It extends the lifetime of a temporary string
quiz.explanation: A view is just pointer + length over existing text: no allocation, no copy, no mutation - and no lifetime extension. If the buffer dies first, the view dangles.

quiz.prompt: Which uses of std::string_view are safe?
options: A function parameter carrying read-only text into a function
Returning a view of a string literal
Returning a view of a local std::string
Storing a view of a longer-lived std::string member
quiz.explanation: String literals and members outlive the view; a local string dies at the end of the function, leaving the view dangling. Parameter use is the canonical safe case.

quiz.prompt: Why is `void scan(std::string_view line)` preferred over `void scan(std::string line)` for hot-path parsing?
quiz.modelAnswer: Passing std::string by value copies the whole buffer (likely allocating), while string_view wraps the existing text with a pointer and length: no allocation, no copy - and it also accepts literals and slices.
quiz.explanation: The view is a borrowed window whose cost is O(1) regardless of text length, which is why C++17 APIs standardised on it for read-only text.

flashcards.back: Passing an array to a function converts it to a pointer to its first element; the length is lost, so APIs carry a separate count parameter.

flashcards.front: Element count of an array in scope
flashcards.back: $\text{count} = \dfrac{\text{sizeof(arr)}}{\text{sizeof(arr[0])}}$ - valid only where the array's true type is known.
C++17 non-owning read-only view: pointer + length over existing text; no allocation; dangles if the underlying buffer dies first.
Array: fixed, contiguous, owned. string: owning, resizable. string_view: borrowing, read-only, cheapest to pass.

flashcards.front: std::string s = "fill"; s += "ed"; then cout << s << ' ' << s.size() prints?
flashcards.back: "filled 6" - += appends in place; size() counts characters.
